name: libuv
summary: A cross-platform asynchronous I/O library centered on a single-threaded event loop, long-lived handles, short-lived requests, and a worker pool for operations without portable nonblocking interfaces.

features.name: Single-threaded cross-platform event loop
features.description: libuv ties an event loop to a single thread, polls nonblocking network sockets through platform-specific mechanisms, and dispatches callbacks through a common loop lifecycle. The design keeps the application-facing execution model consistent while the poller varies by operating system.
benefits: Provides a portable readiness and callback boundary across operating systems
Handles many network events without dedicating a blocking thread to each socket
costs: Loop and handle APIs are generally not thread-safe
Blocking work in the loop thread delays unrelated callbacks

features.name: Handle and request lifecycle
features.description: libuv separates long-lived handles from short-lived requests. Initialized handles are closed asynchronously and their memory may be reclaimed after the close callback; requests carry operation context until completion or cancellation, with operation-specific cleanup where documented.
benefits: Separates persistent event sources from individual operations
Makes callback ownership and cleanup points explicit
costs: Application memory must survive until the documented callback boundary
Different handle and request cleanup rules increase API lifecycle surface

features.name: Thread-pool blocking-operation offload
features.description: libuv uses a global thread pool for filesystem operations, DNS functions, and user-supplied work, while network I/O remains on the loop's thread. Worker completion is reported back through the loop callback model.
benefits: Provides asynchronous APIs for blocking filesystem and resolver operations
Keeps network I/O within the single-threaded event-loop model
costs: The global pool is a bounded shared resource across loops
Work completion and cancellation require coordination between worker and loop contexts

features.name: Opaque handle and stream abstraction
features.description: The public API represents event sources and resources with typed opaque handle structures, and represents many asynchronous operations with typed request structures. Stream APIs use callbacks and buffers to expose common read, write, and connection behavior across TCP, pipes, and related transports.
benefits: Presents common application-facing operations across platform-specific resources
Carries callback context without exposing all internal platform state
costs: Typed lifecycle conventions must be learned for each handle and request family
Opaque internals limit direct control over platform-specific behavior

mathematical_views.question: How do timers, pending callbacks, readiness polling, and close callbacks advance a libuv loop?
assumptions: The loop has active, pending, polling, and closing state components
Callbacks are transitions that may create, stop, or close handles and requests
Platform poller details are abstracted behind readiness events

mathematical_views.question: When may handle and request memory be reclaimed or reused?
assumptions: Handles and requests are distinct resource classes
Close and completion callbacks are ownership transition boundaries
The model excludes application-specific allocation strategies

mathematical_views.question: Which operations remain on the loop thread and which are delegated to worker threads?
assumptions: Network readiness operations are modeled as loop-thread transitions
Filesystem, DNS, and queued user work are modeled as worker-pool jobs whose completions re-enter the loop
The model abstracts pool sizing and operating-system scheduling

costs: Loop affinity and nonblocking handlers constrain application code
Callback-driven cleanup makes premature reuse errors possible

benefits: Nonblocking facade for operations without portable readiness APIs
costs: Shared pool contention and cross-thread completion coordination

benefits: Common transport and callback interfaces across operating systems
costs: Abstraction-specific lifecycle rules add API learning and integration cost
